enrichment.short_title: Whether insolvency-triggered patent divestiture clause was void as against creditors
key_facts: Minority shareholders in Easyrad Limited brought a derivative action alleging UK patent No. 2314391 (the Oyster/BSP Converter) remained Easyrad's property because a 22 October 1998 assignment to Paul Davidson was ineffective.

The assignment was purportedly executed under the 16 October 1997 Easyrad Insolvency Agreement, which allowed Davidson to terminate and recover patents if Easyrad was unable to pay its debts within the meaning of section 123 Insolvency Act 1986.
Easyrad had acquired the patent from Lancashire Fittings for deferred consideration of about £60,000; the patent later underpinned Oystertec PLC's successful AIM flotation raising £30 million.

Claimants accepted Easyrad was balance-sheet insolvent for summary judgment purposes but argued the divestiture clause was void as contrary to public policy and in any event did not cover this patent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for summary judgment in Chancery proceedings following a six-day hearing on the 'Void Transfer' issue in a derivative action permitted by Pumfrey J.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeeded on summary judgment that the Easyrad Assignment did not divest Easyrad of the patent, but the court would refuse a declaration of ownership because of laches/acquiescence; accord and satisfaction and remaining equitable defences reserved for further argument.
enrichment.ratio: An agreement allowing a company to be peremptorily stripped of a principal asset held out to the world as its own property, triggered by balance-sheet insolvency without court process, is to that extent null and void as contrary to the public policy rule in Money Markets Ltd v London Stock Exchange; separately, clause 1 of the Easyrad Insolvency Agreement required transfer for £1 and did not cover a patent acquired for £50,000 plus VAT.
legal_issues: Whether clause 3 required a court determination of insolvency before exercise
Whether the deprivation provision was void as an attempt to contract out of insolvency law
Whether the patent fell within the scope of the Easyrad Insolvency Agreement
Whether laches or acquiescence barred declaratory relief despite voidness
Whether the alternative voidable/fiduciary breach claim could succeed on summary judgment

enrichment.short_title: Inspector's refusal of garden retail use retention upheld on TPO and reasons grounds
key_facts: Mr Evans, acting in person, sought to quash an inspector's decision dismissing an appeal against refusal of permission to retain sale and display of retail A1/garden goods until 30 September 2007.
The site was already used for garden goods; protected trees were covered by a 1991 area Tree Preservation Order and a 1996 woodland order.
At the hearing the parties had negotiated draft landscaping and archaeological conditions that the council would want if permission were granted.
The inspector refused permission mainly because continued use would harm character and appearance and risk loss of important tree cover.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to the High Court to quash a planning inspector's appeal decision; claimant limited argument to two grounds at hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused; Secretary of State's costs assessed at £4,345.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector does not exceed her powers by treating an unrevised area TPO as a material consideration and refusing permission on amenity/tree-cover grounds; where the appellant did not argue that agreed draft conditions would overcome the identified harms, failure to discuss those conditions did not render the reasons inadequate.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector acted beyond her powers in relying on the area TPO
Whether failure to address negotiated draft conditions amounted to inadequate reasons
Whether the local planning authority's failure to resurvey the TPO was relevant on section 288 review

notes: Complete commercial court judgment on products liability policy construction.

enrichment.short_title: Contractors All Risks policy did not cover whole-complex cinema profit loss
key_facts: Horbury, a suspended-ceiling subcontractor at a 16-screen Manchester cinema complex, sought Part 8 declarations on the construction of a Contractors All Risks policy with Hampden.
On 21 December 2001 the ceiling of auditorium 6 collapsed due to wrong washers; AMC closed the entire complex until about 25 January 2002 for investigation and remedial works.
Similar defects were found in other auditoria; Galliford and AMC indicated claims for whole-complex loss of revenue, repair costs and marketing expenses.
The central dispute was whether indemnity extended to loss of profits from closure of cinemas other than auditorium 6.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on assumed and agreed facts before no third-party claim had reached judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Proposed declaration (6) on whole-complex lost profits refused; other sought declarations held unnecessary or not in dispute; question of appropriateness of declarations on hypothetical facts not decided.
enrichment.ratio: Under the products liability indemnity, cover requires physical damage to material property and liability at law for damages in respect of that damage; closure of the rest of the complex for safety inspection and remedial work was not a physical consequence of the collapse in auditorium 6 and therefore associated profit losses were not covered, following A S Screenprint and Rodan.
legal_issues: Whether the cinema complex as a whole was 'Property' damaged by the collapsed ceiling
Whether lost profits from closure of unaffected auditoria were damages in respect of physical damage
Whether Hampden's liability was co-extensive with Horbury's liability to third parties
Whether declarations on partly assumed facts were appropriate before third-party liability was established

notes: Complete section 288 judgment on misinterpretation of Wiltshire development plan policies.

enrichment.short_title: Inspector wrongly treated Holt site outside VPL as countryside barred by policy H5
key_facts: Rosy Homes sought permission for twenty dwellings plus office/workshop units on a disused factory site at Holt, West Wiltshire.
The inspector accepted the form of development would enhance the adjoining conservation area but refused permission as contrary to structure plan policy DP15 and district plan policies including H5.
The appeal site lay within the village of Holt but outside the defined Village Policy Limit (VPL).
The inspector treated paragraph 3.2.29 of the district plan as explanatory of H5 and concluded residential development outside the VPL should be resisted as countryside development.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash a planning inspector's refusal of permission.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed and remitted for reconsideration; claimant's costs assessed at £6,657.10; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 3.2.29 relates to policies H7 and H7A, not H5; policy H5 permits limited development within defined VPLs but is silent on land within an H5 village but outside the VPL, so the inspector erred in rewriting H5 to resist such development; separately, DP15 controls open countryside and could not properly be applied to a site agreed not to be open countryside.
legal_issues: Proper construction of district plan policy H5 outside VPLs
Whether explanatory paragraph 3.2.29 formed part of the development plan and how it should be used
Whether structure plan policy DP15 applied to land within but outside a village boundary
Effect of section 54A where development plan policies were misapplied

enrichment.short_title: 1955 planning grant limited to part of site, not a condition on whole curtilage
key_facts: Mr Payne obtained a continuing planning permission linked to a 21 December 1955 National Coal Board permission for tipping on his land.
The 1955 decision document stated permission was granted for areas AA and EE but not for BB, CC and DD, citing amenity reasons for refusing tipping on the latter areas.
Payne argued the BB/CC/DD restriction was a condition on a permission covering the whole curtilage and fell away once new conditions were imposed under the Environment Act 1995 process.
Maurice Kay J and the Court of Appeal held the 1955 document granted permission only for part of the land and granted no permission at all for BB, CC and DD.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against Maurice Kay J's judgment, following earlier remittal by Pill LJ.
enrichment.ratio: The 1955 document must be construed as granting planning permission only for sections AA and EE and refusing permission entirely for sections BB, CC and DD; it was not an overall grant limited by condition, so no conditions could attach to areas never permitted.
legal_issues: Whether the 1955 BB/CC/DD restriction was a planning condition or a refusal of part of the application
Whether limitations on planning permission are permissible
Effect of new conditions under Environment Act 1995 on the geographic scope of the permission

notes: Complete appeal on sentence for assault on court bailiff.

enrichment.short_title: Three-month sentence for stone thrown at bailiff reduced to 21 days
key_facts: Court bailiff Carole Cassidy attended Mr Easthope's home to serve county court papers in injunction proceedings.
After a hostile encounter at the door, Easthope threw a satsuma-sized stone at her car as she drove away, denting the bonnet; the open driver's window meant she feared personal injury.
Judge Altman found the offence proved under section 14 County Courts Act 1984 and imposed the maximum three-month committal.
Easthope had no previous convictions; the judge treated the act as reckless rather than a deliberate attempt to injure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal as of right to the Court of Appeal against committal for assault on an officer of the court under CCR 34 r 1.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentence reduced from three months to 21 days' imprisonment with immediate release; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Assault on a court officer in execution of duty warrants custodial punishment to protect the administration of justice, but where the assault caused no injury, involved recklessness rather than deliberate targeting, and the offender had no prior convictions, the maximum three-month sentence was excessive and 21 days was sufficient.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentence for assault on a court bailiff under section 14 County Courts Act 1984
Whether proceedings were contempt proceedings attracting enhanced protection for court officers
Weight to be given to mitigating factors where maximum sentence was imposed

notes: Complete habeas corpus judgment on reasonableness of immigration detention.

enrichment.short_title: 19-month immigration detention pending DRC removal held reasonable for now
key_facts: Congolese national Badjoko claimed asylum on arrival in June 2000; asylum and appeal routes failed by November 2001.
He was detained from February 2002 pending removal; two removal attempts in October 2002 failed due to disruptive behaviour and airline refusal.
Documentation difficulties with DRC returns and the claimant's intermittent refusal to cooperate with emergency travel documents prolonged detention.
By the hearing, removal was scheduled for 30 September 2003 with flight, escorts and ticket arranged and DRC representatives promising travel documents within 14 days.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for writ of habeas corpus challenging lawfulness of continued immigration detention.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no order as to costs; judge indicated a different view would be justified if imminent removal plans failed.
enrichment.ratio: Detention under Schedule 3 paragraph 2(3) Immigration Act 1971 must be for the purpose of removal and only for a period reasonably necessary; applying Hardial Singh and I v SSHD, prolonged detention may be reasonable where removal was frustrated by the detainee's own conduct and lack of cooperation, but only while removal within a very short time is realistically achievable.
legal_issues: Whether 19 months' detention exceeded a reasonable period for removal
Effect of claimant's resistance to removal and refusal to cooperate with travel documentation
Risk of absconding if released
Secretary of State's diligence in securing DRC returns by charter flight

notes: Complete section 288 judgment quashing conservatory permission for failure on policy HSG 2.9.

enrichment.short_title: Conservatory permission quashed where inspector did not find exceptional circumstances
key_facts: Neighbour Mrs Taussig challenged an inspector's decision allowing a conservatory at the rear of a ground-floor flat at 28 Southwood Lawn Road, Highgate Conservation Area.

The building was a converted Victorian house divided into seven flats; local plan policy HSG 2.9 normally refused extensions to converted properties unless exceptional circumstances were demonstrated.
The inspector recited HSG 2.9 but did not identify any exceptional circumstances, instead asking whether allowing the extension would undermine the policy's purpose.
Supplementary Planning Guidance SPG 2.4 was not before the inspector because the council failed to provide it in the written representations appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application by adjoining flat owner to quash planning appeal decision allowed on written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed and remitted on the HSG 2.9 ground; SPG ground rejected; claimant's costs assessed at £9,966.58; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under policy HSG 2.9 the inspector had to decide whether exceptional circumstances justified an extension to a converted property; asking only whether granting permission would undermine the policy's purpose was the wrong question and, following Horsham, rendered the decision unlawful even if a departure from the plan might otherwise have been justified.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector applied policy HSG 2.9 by asking the correct question about exceptional circumstances
Whether failure to consider SPG 2.4 invalidated the decision
Whether an inspector must seek out material supplementary guidance not placed before him in a written representations appeal

enrichment.short_title: Oak Mere scheme quashed for failure to weigh drainage benefit to conservation lake
key_facts: Land and Development Ltd appealed against refusal of permission for about 40–50 dwellings and B1 office use in a refurbished courthouse on a 3.233 hectare site at Oak Mere, Cheshire.
The Secretary of State recovered the appeal because of potential effects on adjoining conservation lake Oak Mere.
The inspector found existing drainage from the industrially used site had contributed to nutrient enrichment of the Mere and that proposed diversion could be a substantive benefit.
The Secretary of State refused permission on development plan and visual impact grounds and did not investigate or weigh that drainage benefit because other grounds sufficed for refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to Secretary of State decision rejecting inspector's recommendation to allow the appeal after a reopened inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed and remitted on the drainage-benefit ground alone; other grounds rejected; claimant awarded 50% of costs assessed at £6,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where jurisdiction was recovered because of the importance and vulnerability of Oak Mere, a potential substantive benefit from diverting existing harmful drainage away from the Mere was a material consideration which the Secretary of State was required to investigate and weigh; failure to do so meant there was a real possibility the decision would have differed.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State adequately weighed benefits of the scheme including drainage improvement to Oak Mere
Whether housing supply under the structure plan beyond 2006 had to be considered
Whether reliance on a quashed earlier inspector's visual impact assessment was an immaterial consideration
Whether the visual impact conclusion was perverse

key_facts: Following removal and return of a two-week-old child on 22 June 2001, Sumner J directed a costs schedule process after a hearing on 26 June 2001.

enrichment.outcome: Application adjourned on notice to the respondent; stay ordered; parties directed to mediation via the court ADR service if requested; transcript to be supplied at public expense.
enrichment.ratio: Where permission to appeal raises disputed service and notice issues requiring factual inquiry, and the costs dispute is disproportionate to the sums involved, adjournment with encouragement to mediate is appropriate rather than immediate determination on conflicting untested evidence.
